knowledge_statements.title: Directed Arc-Capacitated Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard single-commodity directed source-sink network model with nonnegative arc flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directed arc-capacitated network is a tuple \(G=(V,A,u,s,t)\), where \(s\ne t\), each arc \(a\in A\) has capacity \(u_a\ge0\), and a feasible flow is \(f\in\mathbb R_+^A\) satisfying \(0\le f_a\le u_a\). With divergence \(\operatorname{div}_f(v)=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a\), conservation requires \(\operatorname{div}_f(v)=0\) for \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\). Its value is \(\nu=\operatorname{div}_f(s)=-\operatorname{div}_f(t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed network assigns nonnegative capacity-bounded flow to each arc, conserves flow at nonterminals, and measures value by net source outflow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le f\le u,\quad \operatorname{div}_f|_{V\setminus\{s,t\}}=0,\quad \nu=\operatorname{div}_f(s)=-\operatorname{div}_f(t)\).

notation.meaning: Arcs leaving and entering vertex v.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be undirected with capacities \(u_e\ge0\), and fix an arbitrary reference orientation of every edge. Let \(B\) be the incidence matrix having \(B_{ve}=1\) when \(v\) is the tail of reference-oriented edge \(e\), \(B_{ve}=-1\) when \(v\) is its head, and \(B_{ve}=0\) otherwise. An undirected feasible source-sink flow is a signed vector \(f\in\mathbb R^E\) satisfying \(|f_e|\le u_e\) and \((Bf)_v=0\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\). Its value is \(\nu=(Bf)_s=-(Bf)_t\). Reversing an edge orientation and negating its coordinate leaves the represented physical flow unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After each undirected edge is given a reference orientation, an undirected flow is a signed, capacity-bounded edge vector whose net-outflow incidence imbalance vanishes away from the source and sink.

children.title: Super-Source Construction
children.top_down_role: Aggregation of multiple source terminals into a single-source model.

knowledge_statements.title: Super-Source Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregates multiple supply terminals into one source using artificial incoming arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a directed network \(G=(V,A,u)\) with source set \(S\subseteq V\), add a new vertex \(\sigma\) and arcs \((\sigma,s)\) of capacities \(M_s\) for all \(s\in S\). A flow \(f\) on the original arcs having nonnegative terminal supplies \(b_s=\operatorname{div}_f(s)\) extends to the augmented network by setting \(f_{\sigma s}=b_s\), provided \(b_s\le M_s\). Conversely, restricting any augmented flow conserved at every \(s\in S\) produces the corresponding multi-source flow, and its total supply equals the super-source outflow \(\sum_{s\in S}f_{\sigma s}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add one super-source with an arc to each original source; those arc flows encode the individual supplies and their sum.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq V\) is the set of supply terminals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_{\sigma s}=b_s\quad(s\in S),\qquad \operatorname{div}_f(\sigma)=\sum_{s\in S}b_s\).

notation.meaning: Supply generated at original source s.
Capacity of the artificial arc to s.

children.title: Super-Sink Construction
children.top_down_role: Aggregation of multiple sink terminals into a single-sink model.

knowledge_statements.title: Super-Sink Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregates multiple demand terminals into one sink using artificial outgoing arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a directed network \(G=(V,A,u)\) with sink set \(T\subseteq V\), add a new vertex \(\tau\) and arcs \((t,\tau)\) of capacities \(N_t\) for all \(t\in T\). A flow \(f\) on the original arcs having nonnegative demands \(d_t=-\operatorname{div}_f(t)\) extends by setting \(f_{t\tau}=d_t\), provided \(d_t\le N_t\). Conversely, restricting any augmented flow conserved at every \(t\in T\) produces the corresponding multi-sink flow, and total demand equals the inflow \(\sum_{t\in T}f_{t\tau}\) into the super-sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add one super-sink with an arc from each original sink; those arc flows encode individual demands and their sum.
assumptions_latex: \(T\subseteq V\) is the set of demand terminals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_{t\tau}=d_t\quad(t\in T),\qquad -\operatorname{div}_f(\tau)=\sum_{t\in T}d_t\).

notation.meaning: Demand absorbed at original sink t.
Capacity of the artificial arc from t.

children.title: Capacity-Safe Terminal Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Capacity choices that preserve the intended terminal behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Safe Terminal Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient capacity rule ensuring artificial terminal arcs cannot restrict aggregate throughput.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=\sum_{a\in A}u_a\) for a finite directed network with nonnegative capacities. In a super-source and super-sink reduction, assign every artificial arc capacity at least \(U\), or assign a valid smaller terminal-specific upper bound. Since the value of every feasible flow on the original network is at most \(U\), no artificial arc with capacity \(U\) can exclude an otherwise feasible terminal imbalance. Thus the augmented single-source, single-sink model preserves the feasible original flows and their aggregate objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Giving every artificial terminal arc capacity at least the sum of original capacities is sufficient to prevent aggregation from creating a bottleneck.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is finite and \(u_a\ge0\) for every \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_s\le M_s\ \forall s,\quad d_t\le N_t\ \forall t\) for every feasible original flow.

notation.meaning: Sum of all original arc capacities.

children.title: Reduction Equivalence Boundary
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing correspondence between original and reduced instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction Equivalence Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact aggregation fails when artificial capacities exclude required terminal imbalances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For artificial capacities \(M_s\) and \(N_t\), restriction from the augmented network yields exactly those original feasible flows satisfying \(b_s\le M_s\) and \(d_t\le N_t\). Hence feasible-set equivalence requires these inequalities for every original feasible flow; optimum-value equivalence requires them for at least one original optimum. The boundary is sharp: if the original network consists of one arc \((s,t)\) of capacity \(2\), while \((\sigma,s)\) has capacity \(1\) and \((t,\tau)\) capacity \(2\), the original optimum is \(2\) but the reduced optimum is \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregation is exact only when artificial arcs admit the relevant terminal imbalances; an undersized arc can strictly lower the optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{restricted}}=\{f\in\mathcal F: b_s\le M_s\ \forall s,\ d_t\le N_t\ \forall t\}\).

notation.meaning: Source supplies and sink demands induced by a flow.

source_refs.locator: Section 5. Combinatorial Implications of Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem p. 120

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\subseteq V\) be a set of conserved vertices in a finite directed network \(G=(V,A)\), and let each \(v\in W\) have throughput capacity \(c_v\ge0\). For every \(v\in W\), replace \(v\) by \(v^{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(v^{\mathrm{out}}\), add the arc \((v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}})\) of capacity \(c_v\), redirect every original arc entering \(v\) to \(v^{\mathrm{in}}\), and redirect every original arc leaving \(v\) from \(v^{\mathrm{out}}\). Conservation at the two copies forces the splitting-arc flow to equal both the total original inflow and the total original outflow at \(v\). Restriction and extension therefore give a value-preserving correspondence between flows satisfying these vertex-throughput capacities and ordinary arc-capacitated flows in the split network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split each conserved capacitated vertex into input and output copies connected by an arc whose flow equals the vertex's conserved throughput.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), an arc-flow coordinate vector is \(f=(f_a)_{a\in A}\in\mathbb R^A\). Under the nonnegative directed-flow convention, feasibility with lower bounds \(\ell\in\mathbb R_+^A\) and upper capacities \(u\in\mathbb R_+^A\), where \(\ell\le u\), means \(\ell_a\le f_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\). Each coordinate records the amount sent in the prescribed direction of its arc; balance constraints are imposed separately through the incidence map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative directed flow is represented by one real coordinate per arc, subject to componentwise nonnegative lower bounds and upper capacities.

children.title: Vertex Divergence Profiles
children.top_down_role: Vertex-level net-flow information induced by arc assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Divergence Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear image of arc-flow coordinates under the directed incidence operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix the divergence-sign incidence matrix \(B\in\{-1,0,1\}^{V\times A}\), with \(B_{va}=1\) when arc \(a\) leaves \(v\), \(B_{va}=-1\) when it enters \(v\), and \(B_{va}=0\) otherwise. The vertex divergence profile represented by an arc-flow vector \(f\in\mathbb R^A\) is \(b=Bf\), so \(b_v=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a\). Every such profile satisfies \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), because each arc contributes once with each sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying arc-flow coordinates by the signed incidence matrix gives each vertex's net outflow, whose total is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b=Bf,\qquad b_v=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a,\qquad \sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).

notation.meaning: Incidence matrix using the net-outflow sign convention.
Outgoing and incoming arcs at v.

children.title: Conservation Interface
children.top_down_role: Relationship between arc coordinates and vertex balance conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Conservation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balance condition linking arc coordinates to prescribed supplies and demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\) use the net-outflow sign convention and let \(b\in\mathbb R^V\) prescribe vertex supplies and demands. An arc-flow vector \(f\) satisfies the conservation interface exactly when \(Bf=b\). Thus vertices with \(b_v=0\) conserve flow, vertices with \(b_v>0\) generate net supply, and vertices with \(b_v<0\) absorb net demand. The compatibility condition \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\) is necessary. For a source-sink flow of value \(
u\), this specializes to \(b_s=
u\), \(b_t=-
u\), and \(b_v=0\) elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conservation equates incidence times the arc-flow vector with the prescribed supply-demand profile; zero-profile vertices conserve flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Bf=b,\qquad \sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).

notation.meaning: Divergence profile induced by the arc flow.
Prescribed net supply at vertex v.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacitated Flows, Excess, Circulations, and Source–Sink Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical nonnegative single-commodity arc flows, using excess equal to inflow minus outflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a digraph and \(u:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{+}\). A flow is a function \(f:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{+}\) satisfying \(f(e)\le u(e)\) for every \(e\in E(G)\). Its excess at \(v\in V(G)\) is \(\operatorname{ex}_{f}(v):=\sum_{e\in\delta^{-}(v)}f(e)-\sum_{e\in\delta^{+}(v)}f(e)\). The flow satisfies conservation at \(v\) when \(\operatorname{ex}_{f}(v)=0\), and it is a circulation when conservation holds at every vertex. Given a network \((G,u,s,t)\), an \(s\)-\(t\) flow is a flow satisfying \(\operatorname{ex}_{f}(s)\le 0\) and \(\operatorname{ex}_{f}(v)=0\) for every \(v\in V(G)\setminus\{s,t\}\). Its value is \(\operatorname{value}(f):=-\operatorname{ex}_{f}(s)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flow assigns every edge a nonnegative amount no greater than its capacity. Excess is inflow minus outflow. Zero excess is conservation, and a flow conserved at every vertex is a circulation. An s–t flow is conserved away from the source and sink, has nonpositive source excess, and has value equal to the negative source excess.
assumptions_latex: s,t\in V(G)\text{ for the source--sink specialization}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{+},\ f\le u;\quad \operatorname{ex}_{f}(v)=\sum_{e\in\delta^{-}(v)}f(e)-\sum_{e\in\delta^{+}(v)}f(e);\quad f\text{ is a circulation}\iff \operatorname{ex}_{f}(v)=0\ \forall v;\quad \operatorname{value}(f)=-\operatorname{ex}_{f}(s)\text{ for an }s\text{-}t\text{ flow}.

Let \(f\in\mathbb R_+^A\) be a feasible source-sink flow on a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), with divergence \(Bf=
u\mathbf e_s-
u\mathbf e_t\) and value \(
u\ge0\). Then \(f\) can be written as \(f=\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i\chi^{P_i}+g\), where each \(P_i\) is a simple directed source-to-sink path, each \(\lambda_i>0\), and \(g\in\mathbb R_+^A\) is a circulation. The path coefficients carry the entire flow value: \(\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i=

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Augmenting-Path Maximum-Flow Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum flow in a finite capacitated directed network with source 1 and sink m.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible flow $x$ with $0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}$, form a residual digraph containing $(i,j)$ with residual capacity $u_{ij}-x_{ij}$ whenever $x_{ij}<u_{ij}$ and $(j,i)$ with residual capacity $x_{ij}$ whenever $x_{ij}>0$. If a residual $1$–$m$ path $P$ exists, let $\Delta$ be its minimum residual capacity, increase by $\Delta$ the original-arc flows traversed forward, decrease by $\Delta$ those traversed backward, and repeat. If no residual $1$–$m$ path exists, terminate; the current flow is maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from a feasible flow, construct its residual network, and repeatedly augment along a source-to-sink residual path by the path's bottleneck capacity, increasing forward-arc flows and decreasing backward-arc flows. When no such path exists, the current flow is maximum.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is a finite directed network with source }1\text{ and sink }m.
x\text{ is a feasible flow satisfying conservation and }0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{If the residual graph contains no }1\text{–}m\text{ path, then }x\text{ is a maximum flow.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Labeling Algorithm for Maximum Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit residual-path construction by predecessor and bottleneck labels, including a minimum-cut certificate at termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $x_{ij}=0$ and, in each iteration, label the source by $L(1)=(-,\infty)$. From a labeled node $i$, label an unlabeled node $j$ by $(+i,\min\{\Delta_i,u_{ij}-x_{ij}\})$ when $x_{ij}<u_{ij}$, or by $(-i,\min\{\Delta_i,x_{ji}\})$ when $x_{ji}>0$. If the sink $m$ is labeled, set $\Delta=\Delta_m$, backtrack through the predecessor labels, augmenting forward-labeled arcs and reducing backward-labeled arcs by $\Delta$, erase the labels, and repeat. If $m$ cannot be labeled, terminate: the current flow is maximum, and the cut $(X,V\setminus X)$ determined by the labeled-node set $X$ is a minimum-capacity cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Labels record a predecessor, direction, and the largest feasible bottleneck from the source. If the sink is labeled, backtrack through the labels and augment by its bottleneck value. If the sink cannot be labeled, the flow is maximum and the labeled nodes define a minimum cut.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is a finite directed network with source }1\text{ and sink }m.
x_{ij}=0\text{ initially, and every update maintains flow conservation and }0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m\notin X\implies x\text{ is a maximum flow and }(X,V\setminus X)\text{ is a minimum-capacity cut.}

children.title: Circulation Cycle Components
children.top_down_role: Flow components supported on directed cycles.

knowledge_statements.title: Circulation Cycle Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle decomposition of a finite nonnegative circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every nonnegative circulation \(g\in\mathbb R_+^A\) on a finite directed graph has a decomposition \(g=\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_j\chi^{C_j}\), where each \(C_j\) is a simple directed cycle and each \(\mu_j>0\). The cycles may be chosen from the positive-support subgraph of \(g\). Iteratively selecting such a cycle and subtracting the minimum flow on its arcs eliminates at least one positive arc, so a representation exists with \(q\le |A|\). Each cycle component has zero divergence and therefore does not change any source-sink flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite nonnegative circulation is a positive sum of simple directed cycle flows, with at most one component per arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g=\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_j\chi^{C_j},\qquad \mu_j>0,\qquad q\le |A|,\qquad B\chi^{C_j}=0\).

notation.meaning: Positive weight of the cycle component.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circulations, simple cycle circulations, and cycle pushes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a circulation and the signed simple circulation associated with a cycle, together with cycle cost and the cost change under a cycle push. The push is not asserted to preserve capacity or other feasibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A flow vector \(f\), whether feasible or infeasible, is a circulation if \(Af=0\). For a cycle \(C\), fix a traversal and let \(F\) and \(B\) denote the arcs oriented with and against that traversal. Define \(h^C_{ij}=1\) for \((i,j)\in F\), \(h^C_{ij}=-1\) for \((i,j)\in B\), and \(h^C_{ij}=0\) otherwise. Then \(Ah^C=0\), so \(h^C\) is the simple circulation associated with \(C\). Its cost is \(c^\top h^C=\sum_{(i,j)\in F}c_{ij}-\sum_{(i,j)\in B}c_{ij}\). Pushing \(\theta\) units around \(C\) replaces \(f\) by \(f+\theta h^C\) and changes the linear cost by \(\theta c^\top h^C\); this identity alone does not guarantee feasibility of the resulting flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flow vector is a circulation when its net flow imbalance is zero at every node, regardless of whether it otherwise satisfies feasibility constraints. Traversing a cycle defines a signed cycle flow that is itself a circulation. Its cost is the sum of costs on forward arcs minus the sum on backward arcs, and adding theta times this cycle flow changes the linear cost by theta times the cycle cost. Such a push need not preserve capacities or other feasibility conditions.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is the node-arc incidence matrix and }f\text{ is a flow vector.}
C\text{ is a cycle with a fixed traversal, with forward-arc set }F\text{ and backward-arc set }B.
c\text{ is the arc-cost vector and }\theta\in\mathbb{R}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ah^C=0,\qquad c^\top(f+\theta h^C)-c^\top f=\theta c^\top h^C=\theta\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in F}c_{ij}-\sum_{(i,j)\in B}c_{ij}\right).

children.title: Decomposition Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Structural variation among valid component decompositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of path-component representations even when the represented arc flow is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Path-flow decompositions need not be unique. Consider arcs from \(s\) to \(a,b\), from \(a,b\) to \(v\), from \(v\) to \(c,d\), and from \(c,d\) to \(t\). Assign one unit of flow to every arc. The resulting arc flow equals the sum of the incidence vectors of the two paths \(s,a,v,c,t\) and \(s,b,v,d,t\), but it also equals the sum of the incidence vectors of \(s,a,v,d,t\) and \(s,b,v,c,t\). Thus distinct multisets of source-sink paths can induce the same arc-flow vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed arc flow can have distinct path decompositions because paths may be paired differently after flows merge and before they split.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is the finite directed graph specified in the statement.
Each displayed path carries one unit of flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi^{s a v c t}+\chi^{s b v d t}=\chi^{s a v d t}+\chi^{s b v c t}\).

notation.meaning: arc-incidence vector of directed path P

knowledge_statements.title: Conformal Flow Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sign-compatible decomposition into elementary paths and directed cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^A\), and let \(b=\operatorname{div}x\), where divergence is outflow minus inflow in the original orientation. Form the sign-support digraph \(H_x\) by retaining each arc \(a=(v,w)\) with \(x_a>0\) in the direction \(v\to w\), reversing it when \(x_a<0\), and omitting it when \(x_a=0\). Then there are finite index sets \(I,J\), positive coefficients \(\alpha_i\) for \(i\in I\) and \(\beta_j\) for \(j\in J\), simple directed paths \(P_i\) in \(H_x\) from vertices with positive \(b\) to vertices with negative \(b\), and simple directed cycles \(C_j\) in \(H_x\) such that \[x=\sum_{i\in I}\alpha_i\chi^{P_i}+\sum_{j\in J}\beta_j\chi^{C_j}.\] Here each incidence vector is signed relative to the original orientation of \(A\), so every summand is conformal to \(x\). If \(b=0\), one may take \(I=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite signed flow decomposes into sign-compatible simple paths from positive-divergence vertices to negative-divergence vertices and sign-compatible simple cycles; a circulation requires only cycles.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}^A\) and \(b=\operatorname{div}x\), with divergence measured in the original arc orientation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) admits a finite conformal path-cycle decomposition, and if \(b=0\), only cycle terms are required.

notation.meaning: support digraph obtained by orienting each nonzero coordinate according to the sign of x relative to the original arc orientation
outflow minus inflow at each vertex in the original orientation

children.title: Forward Residual Capacity
children.top_down_role: Remaining capacity associated with the original arc orientation.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward Residual Capacity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-lower-bound capacitated flows with a separate residual-arc copy for each original arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a=(v,w)\) be an original arc with capacity \(u_a\) and feasible flow \(f_a\). Its forward residual arc is the copy from \(v\) to \(w\) having residual capacity \[r_f^+(a)=u_a-f_a.\] This quantity is the largest \(\delta\ge 0\) by which \(f_a\) can be increased while retaining the upper-capacity constraint. The forward residual arc is present in the residual network exactly when \(r_f^+(a)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc's forward residual capacity is its unused capacity, and the forward residual arc exists precisely when that amount is positive.

children.title: Reverse Residual Capacity
children.top_down_role: Reversible capacity associated with previously assigned flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Reverse Residual Capacity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cancellation capacity for a zero-lower-bound flow on an original directed arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a=(v,w)\) be an original arc carrying feasible flow \(f_a\). Its reverse residual arc is the residual copy from \(w\) to \(v\) with capacity \[r_f^-(a)=f_a.\] This is the largest \(\delta\ge 0\) by which the flow on \(a\) may be decreased without violating its zero lower bound. The reverse residual arc is present exactly when \(f_a>0\), independently of whether an original arc from \(w\) to \(v\) also exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc's reverse residual capacity equals its current flow and measures how much of that flow can be canceled.

notation.meaning: current flow on original arc a
reverse residual capacity associated with a

children.title: Residual Cancellation Interface
children.top_down_role: Interaction between opposite residual orientations during flow revision.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Cancellation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of residual-path augmentation into increases or cancellations on original arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a directed simple path in the residual multigraph and let \(0\le\delta\le\min_{e\in P}r_f(e)\). Define \(f'\) by adding \(\delta\) to each original arc traversed through its forward residual copy and subtracting \(\delta\) from each original arc traversed through its reverse residual copy. Then \(f'\) respects all original arc bounds. At each internal vertex of \(P\), the change in inflow equals the change in outflow, so augmentation changes divergence only at the endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Traversing a reverse residual arc cancels original flow; augmenting a simple residual path by at most its bottleneck preserves arc bounds and conservation at internal vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is feasible for zero lower bounds and upper capacities \(u\).
\(P\) is a directed simple path in the residual multigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le f'\le u\), and the divergence of every internal vertex of \(P\) is unchanged.

notation.meaning: original-arc flow obtained after the residual-path augmentation

children.title: Residual Path Families
children.top_down_role: Navigable path structures within a residual network.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Path Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Families of directed paths supported by positive-capacity residual arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible flow \(f\), let \(G_f=(V,A_f)\) be its residual multigraph, where \(A_f\) contains exactly the residual-arc copies having positive residual capacity. For vertices \(x,y\in V\), define the residual path family by \[\mathcal{P}_f(x,y)=\{P:P\text{ is a directed simple }x\text{-}y\text{ path in }G_f\}.\] Each \(P\in\mathcal{P}_f(x,y)\) has bottleneck \(r_f(P)=\min_{e\in P}r_f(e)>0\). Consequently, augmenting along \(P\) by any \(\delta\) satisfying \(0\le\delta\le r_f(P)\) preserves all original arc bounds, while changing divergence only at \(x\) and \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual path family consists of simple directed paths whose residual arcs have positive capacity; augmentation up to a path's bottleneck preserves arc bounds and affects divergence only at its endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\in\mathcal{P}_f(x,y)\Rightarrow r_f(P)>0\).

notation.meaning: family of simple residual paths from x to y

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Network, Flow Augmentation, and Augmenting Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational residual-network definitions for capacitated directed flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a digraph $G$, form $\overleftrightarrow G$ by adjoining to every $e=(v,w)\in E(G)$ a distinct reverse edge $\overleftarrow e=(w,v)$; a pre-existing antiparallel edge remains distinct from $\overleftarrow e$. Given capacities $u:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+$ and a flow $f$, define $u_f(e)=u(e)-f(e)$ and $u_f(\overleftarrow e)=f(e)$ for $e\in E(G)$, and define $G_f=(V(G),\{a\in E(\overleftrightarrow G):u_f(a)>0\})$. Augmenting $f$ along a path or circuit $P\subseteq G_f$ by $\gamma$ increases $f(e)$ by $\gamma$ on forward edges and decreases $f(e)$ by $\gamma$ on corresponding reverse edges. For a network $(G,u,s,t)$, an $f$-augmenting path is an $s$-$t$ path in $G_f$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual graph contains positive-residual-capacity forward and reverse arcs. Augmentation adds flow on forward arcs and removes flow on reverse arcs; an augmenting path is a source-to-sink path in this graph.
assumptions_latex: u:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+\text{ and }f\text{ is a feasible flow}
P\text{ is a path or circuit in }G_f
0\leq\gamma\leq\min_{a\in E(P)}u_f(a)\text{ when feasibility is to be preserved}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G_f=(V(G),\{a:u_f(a)>0\}),\qquad P\text{ is }f\text{-augmenting}\iff P\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ path in }G_f.

children.title: Source-Reachable Region
children.top_down_role: Vertices accessible from the source through residual capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Source-Reachable Region
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reachability from the source in the positive-capacity residual multigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible flow \(f\) with source \(s\), its source-reachable region is \[S_f=\{v\in V:v=s\text{ or }\mathcal{P}_f(s,v)\ne\varnothing\}.\] Equivalently, \(S_f\) is the smallest vertex set containing \(s\) that is closed under heads of positive-capacity residual arcs: if \(v\in S_f\) and \((v,w)\in A_f\), then \(w\in S_f\). In particular, an augmenting source-sink path exists exactly when \(t\in S_f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The source-reachable region contains precisely the vertices reachable from the source through positive-capacity residual arcs; it contains the sink exactly when augmentation is possible.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a feasible flow with source \(s\) and sink \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\in S_f\iff\mathcal{P}_f(s,t)\ne\varnothing\).

children.title: Sink-Separating Frontier
children.top_down_role: Boundary induced when residual reachability excludes the sink.

knowledge_statements.title: Sink-Separating Frontier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-reachability certificate producing a saturated source-sink cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow and suppose \(t\notin S_f\). Then \((S_f,V\setminus S_f)\) is an \(s\)-\(t\) cut with no positive-capacity residual arc leaving \(S_f\). Consequently every original arc leaving \(S_f\) is saturated, and every original arc entering \(S_f\) carries zero flow. These locally checkable conditions give \[|f|=u(\delta^+(S_f)),\] so the frontier \(\delta^+(S_f)\) certifies simultaneously that \(f\) is maximum and that the displayed cut is minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the sink is not residual-reachable, the reachable-set frontier is a saturated cut whose capacity equals the flow value, certifying optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|f|=u(\delta^+(S_f))\), hence \(f\) is maximum and \((S_f,V\setminus S_f)\) is minimum.

notation.meaning: sum of capacities of arcs leaving S

children.title: Residual Distance Layers
children.top_down_role: Distance-based partitioning of vertices in residual networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Distance Layers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Breadth-first layers of the residual multigraph measured toward a designated sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a sink \(t\) in the residual multigraph \(G_f\). Define \(d_f(v)\) as the minimum number of residual arcs in a directed path from \(v\) to \(t\), with value \(\infty\) if no such path exists. The residual distance layers are \[L_k=\{v\in V:d_f(v)=k\},\qquad k=0,1,\ldots,|V|-1.\] Thus \(L_0=\{t\}\), and for every vertex with finite positive distance, \(v\in L_k\) exactly when it has a residual arc to some vertex of \(L_{k-1}\) and no path to \(t\) using fewer than \(k\) arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual distance layers partition sink-reachable vertices by the minimum number of positive-capacity residual arcs needed to reach the sink.

notation.meaning: directed residual distance from v to t

children.title: Valid Distance Labels
children.top_down_role: Label structures compatible with residual accessibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Valid Distance Labels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible lower-bound labels for directed residual distance to the sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(d:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\cup\{\infty\}\) is a valid sink-distance labeling of a residual multigraph \(G_f=(V,A_f)\) if \[d(t)=0\quad\text{and}\quad d(v)\le d(w)+1\quad\text{for every }(v,w)\in A_f,\] using \(\infty+1=\infty\). Along any residual path from \(v\) to \(t\), repeated application gives \(d(v)\) no larger than the path length. Hence every finite valid label is a lower bound on the exact residual distance to \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid label assigns zero to the sink and can decrease by at most one along any residual arc; finite labels lower-bound true sink distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(v)\le d_f(v)\) for every \(v\) with finite \(d(v)\).

notation.meaning: exact residual distance from v to t

children.title: Unreachable-Vertex Labels
children.top_down_role: Label treatment for vertices outside relevant residual reachability.

knowledge_statements.title: Unreachable-Vertex Labels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite and finite-sentinel encodings of vertices having no residual path to the sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For exact residual distance to a fixed sink \(t\), assign \(d_f(v)=\infty\) precisely when \(\mathcal{P}_f(v,t)=\varnothing\). Because every shortest path in a finite graph may be chosen simple, every finite distance is at most \(|V|-1\). Therefore the finite sentinel \(D_f(v)=\min\{d_f(v),|V|\}\) represents unreachable vertices exactly by \(D_f(v)=|V|\), without colliding with any finite exact distance. The infinity-valued and sentinel-valued representations consequently encode the same reachability partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex is labeled infinity when it cannot reach the sink residually; the sentinel number of vertices gives an equivalent finite encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{P}_f(v,t)=\varnothing\iff d_f(v)=\infty\iff D_f(v)=|V|\).

notation.meaning: distance capped at the sentinel value |V|

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Source-Sink Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity of an ordered source-side partition in a directed capacitated graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed graph with nonnegative arc capacities \(u\) and distinct vertices \(s,t\). A directed \(s\)-\(t\) cut is a set \(S\subseteq V\) satisfying \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\), together with its forward boundary \[\delta^+(S)=\{(v,w)\in A:v\in S,\ w\notin S\}.\] Its capacity is \(u(\delta^+(S))=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_a\). Arcs entering \(S\) are not included in this directed cut capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed source-sink cut is a vertex set containing the source but not the sink; its capacity sums only arcs leaving that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u(S,V\setminus S)=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_a\).

notation.meaning: arcs directed from S to its complement

knowledge_statements.title: Undirected Cut Partitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The standard bipartition representation of a cut in a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. For every nonempty proper subset \(S\subset V\), the ordered pair \((S,V\setminus S)\) determines a cut partition, whose crossing-edge set is
\[\delta(S)=\{\{u,v\}\in E: u\in S,\ v\in V\setminus S\}.\]
As an unoriented cut, the two shores are interchangeable: \(\delta(S)=\delta(V\setminus S)\), so \(S\) and \(V\setminus S\) represent the same cut. For distinct terminals \(s,t\in V\), it is an \(s\)-\(t\) cut when \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nontrivial vertex bipartition defines the edges crossing between its shores; complementary shores represent the same undirected cut, with terminal cuts separating the designated vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta(S)=\delta(V\setminus S)\), and \((S,V\setminus S)\) is an \(s\)-\(t\) cut exactly when \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\).

notation.meaning: Set of edges having exactly one endpoint in S.

children.title: Cut-Capacity Functions
children.top_down_role: Set functions induced by capacities crossing cut boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Capacity Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted undirected cut capacity as a set function on vertex subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with edge capacities \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\). Its cut-capacity function is the set function \(d_c:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) defined by
\[d_c(S)=c(\delta(S))=\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c(e)\qquad(S\subseteq V).\]
Thus \(d_c(\varnothing)=d_c(V)=0\), and complementary vertex sets have equal capacity: \(d_c(S)=d_c(V\setminus S)\). When terminals \(s,t\) are fixed, the capacity of an \(s\)-\(t\) cut is \(d_c(S)\) for \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cut-capacity function assigns each vertex set the total capacity of edges with exactly one endpoint in that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_c(S)=\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c(e)\), with \(d_c(S)=d_c(V\setminus S)\) and \(d_c(\varnothing)=d_c(V)=0\).

notation.meaning: Cut-capacity set function induced by c.

children.title: Submodular Cut Structure
children.top_down_role: Submodular organization of cut-capacity values.

knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Cut Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry and submodularity of nonnegative weighted undirected cut functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with capacities \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), the cut-capacity function \(d_c\) is symmetric and submodular. Explicitly, for every \(X,Y\subseteq V\),
\[d_c(X)=d_c(V\setminus X)\]
and
\[d_c(X)+d_c(Y)\ge d_c(X\cap Y)+d_c(X\cup Y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative weighted undirected cut-capacity function is symmetric under complementation and submodular under intersection and union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(X,Y\subseteq V\), \(d_c(X)=d_c(V\setminus X)\) and \(d_c(X)+d_c(Y)\ge d_c(X\cap Y)+d_c(X\cup Y)\).

notation.meaning: Total capacity of the edges crossing S.

children.title: Cut Uncrossing Consequences
children.top_down_role: Cut-family organization supported by submodular structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Uncrossing Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lattice closure of minimum cuts separating a fixed terminal pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d_c\) be the nonnegative weighted cut-capacity function of a finite undirected graph, and fix distinct vertices \(s,t\). If \(X\) and \(Y\) are minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut shores oriented so that \(s\in X\cap Y\) and \(t\notin X\cup Y\), then both \(X\cap Y\) and \(X\cup Y\) are minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut shores. Consequently, the family of minimum shores containing \(s\) is closed under intersection and union and therefore has unique inclusion-minimal and inclusion-maximal members.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting or uniting two consistently oriented minimum source-sink cut shores yields another minimum cut, giving unique smallest and largest minimum shores.
assumptions_latex: \(d_c\) is induced by nonnegative capacities on a finite undirected graph.
\(X\) and \(Y\) are minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut shores containing \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_c(X\cap Y)=d_c(X\cup Y)=d_c(X)=d_c(Y)\), and the minimum \(s\)-side shores form a lattice under \(\cap\) and \(\cup\).

notation.meaning: Minimum cut shores containing s and excluding t.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Source-Sink Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-capacity directed max-flow min-cut theorem with unrestricted real flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(s\ne t\), and let \(c:A\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\). Among all functions \(f:A\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) satisfying \(f(a)\le c(a)\) and flow conservation at every vertex in \(V\setminus\{s,t\}\), the maximum flow value equals the minimum capacity of a directed \(s\)-\(t\) cut:
\[\max_f |f|=\min_{S\subseteq V:\ s\in S,\ t\notin S}\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}c(a).\]
If all capacities are integral, an integral maximum flow exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite capacitated digraph, maximum source-to-sink flow equals minimum outgoing capacity of a separating cut; integral capacities admit an integral optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with distinct \(s,t\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_f |f|=\min_{s\in S,\ t\notin S}c(\delta^+(S))\); moreover, integral \(c\) permits integral optimal \(f\).

knowledge_statements.title: Undirected Source-Sink Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected max-flow min-cut theorem using antisymmetric edge flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with distinct terminals \(s,t\) and capacities \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\). An undirected flow assigns antisymmetric values \(f(u,v)=-f(v,u)\), satisfies \(|f(u,v)|\le c(\{u,v\})\), and conserves flow at every nonterminal vertex. Then
\[\max_f |f|=\min_{S\subseteq V:\ s\in S,\ t\notin S}\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c(e).\]
When all capacities are integral, the maximum is attained by an integral antisymmetric flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum feasible undirected source-to-sink flow equals the minimum capacity of an undirected cut separating the terminals, with integrality for integral capacities.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected with distinct terminals \(s,t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_f |f|=\min_{s\in S,\ t\notin S}c(\delta(S))\), with an integral optimum whenever \(c\) is integral.

notation.meaning: Undirected edges crossing between S and its complement.

children.title: Vertex-Splitting Form

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Splitting Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of internal vertex capacities to ordinary directed arc capacities when every source-to-sink path has an internal vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with distinct terminals \(s,t\), no arc from \(s\) to \(t\), and internal vertex capacities \(b:V\setminus\{s,t\}\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\). Set \(B=\sum_{v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}}b(v)\) and choose \(M>B\). Replace every internal vertex \(v\) by \(v^{\mathrm{in}}\), \(v^{\mathrm{out}}\), and an arc \((v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}})\) of capacity \(b(v)\). Replace every original arc by the corresponding arc from its tail's output copy to its head's input copy, leaving terminals unsplit, and give that arc capacity \(M\). This split network preserves the maximum value of flows whose throughput at each internal vertex \(v\) is at most \(b(v)\). Every minimum split-network cut has capacity at most \(B<M\), crosses no capacity-\(M\) replacement arc, and its crossed split arcs encode a minimum-capacity internal vertex separator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting each internal vertex into input and output copies joined by its capacity arc converts internally vertex-capacitated flow into ordinary arc-capacitated flow; sufficiently large capacities on replacement arcs ensure minimum cuts encode vertex separators.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is finite and directed with distinct terminals \(s,t\).
There is no arc from \(s\) to \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The split network preserves the maximum vertex-capacitated \(s\)-\(t\) flow value, and every minimum cut crosses only arcs \((v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}})\), which encode a minimum-capacity internal vertex separator.

notation.meaning: Throughput capacity of internal vertex v.
Input and output copies of a split internal vertex.
Sum of all internal vertex capacities.
Common capacity assigned to arcs representing original arcs, chosen larger than B.

knowledge_statements.title: Internally Vertex-Disjoint Path Packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The internally vertex-disjoint, nonadjacent-terminal form of Menger's theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let distinct nonadjacent vertices \(s,t\in V\) be connected. The maximum cardinality of a family of \(s\)-\(t\) paths whose internal vertex sets are pairwise disjoint equals the minimum cardinality of a set \(W\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\}\) such that \(s\) and \(t\) lie in different components of \(G-W\):
\[\max\{|\mathcal P|:\mathcal P\text{ is internally vertex-disjoint}\}=\min\{|W|:G-W\text{ separates }s\text{ and }t\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonadjacent terminals, the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint connecting paths equals the minimum number of internal vertices whose deletion separates them.
assumptions_latex: \(s,t\in V\) are distinct, nonadjacent, and connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max |\mathcal P|=\min |W|\), where \(\mathcal P\) ranges over internally vertex-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) path families and \(W\) over internal \(s\)-\(t\) separators.

notation.meaning: Family of internally vertex-disjoint s-t paths.

children.title: Vertex-Cut Dual Form
children.top_down_role: Separating vertex sets corresponding to the packing formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Cut Dual Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-capacitated vertex-path packing versus minimum weighted vertex separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with distinct nonadjacent terminals \(s,t\), and let \(b:V\setminus\{s,t\}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\). A path packing is a multiset \(\mathcal P\) of \(s\)-\(t\) paths in which each internal vertex \(v\) occurs in at most \(b(v)\) paths. Then
\[\max_{\mathcal P}|\mathcal P|=\min_{W}\sum_{v\in W}b(v),\]
where \(W\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\}\) ranges over vertex sets whose deletion separates \(s\) from \(t\). Both optima are integral and are represented respectively by a flow and a cut in the vertex-split network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum integral path packing subject to internal vertex capacities equals the minimum total capacity of a vertex separator.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected, and \(s,t\) are distinct and nonadjacent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{\mathcal P}|\mathcal P|=\min_{W}\sum_{v\in W}b(v)\), with integral optimal packing and separator.

notation.meaning: Multiplicity capacity of internal vertex v.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Reachability Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-flow certificate obtained from vertices reachable in the residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be a feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow in a finite capacitated digraph, and form its residual digraph using forward residual capacities \(c(a)-f(a)\) and reverse residual capacities \(f(a)\). If \(t\) is not reachable from \(s\), let \(R\) be the set of vertices reachable from \(s\). Then \(s\in R\), \(t\notin R\), every original arc leaving \(R\) is saturated, and every original arc entering \(R\) carries zero flow. Hence
\[|f|=c(\delta^+(R)),\]
so \(f\) is maximum and \((R,V\setminus R)\) is a minimum cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the residual network has no source-to-sink path, the source-reachable vertices define a cut whose capacity equals the feasible flow value.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a feasible flow in a finite directed network.
The residual digraph contains no directed \(s\)-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the residual-reachable set \(R\), \(|f|=c(\delta^+(R))\); therefore \(f\) is maximum and \(R\) defines a minimum cut.

notation.meaning: Vertices reachable from s in the residual digraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Saturated-Cut Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality certificate based on saturation and zero reverse flow across a cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be a feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow in a finite directed network and let \(S\subseteq V\) satisfy \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\). If every arc in \(\delta^+(S)\) is saturated, meaning \(f(a)=c(a)\), and every arc in \(\delta^-(S)\) carries zero flow, then flow conservation gives
\[|f|=f(\delta^+(S))-f(\delta^-(S))=c(\delta^+(S)).\]
This equality is a directly checkable certificate that \(f\) is a maximum flow and that \(S\) is a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut shore.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow is maximum when some separating cut has all forward arcs saturated and all backward arcs carrying zero flow.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a feasible flow in a finite directed network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|f|=c(\delta^+(S))\), so \(f\) is maximum and \(S\) is a minimum cut shore.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Value Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality from equality of feasible flow and cut objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a finite directed capacitated network, let \(f\) be any feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow and let \(S\) be any \(s\)-\(t\) cut shore. Weak flow-cut duality gives
\[|f|\le c(\delta^+(S)).\]
Therefore, if the independently checkable primal and dual values coincide,
\[|f|=c(\delta^+(S)),\]
then no feasible flow has value larger than \(|f|\), and no \(s\)-\(t\) cut has capacity smaller than \(c(\delta^+(S))\). The pair \((f,S)\) consequently certifies simultaneously that \(f\) is maximum and \(S\) is minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow and feasible cut with equal objective values jointly certify maximum-flow and minimum-cut optimality by weak duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible pair \((f,S)\) is primal-dual optimal: \(f\) is a maximum flow and \(S\) is a minimum cut shore.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Source-Side Minimum Cut
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the unique inclusion-minimal source side using any maximum flow's residual graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite capacitated digraph with distinct vertices \(s,t\), nonnegative capacities \(u\), and a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow \(f\). Let \(G_f\) be its residual graph and let \(S_{\min}\) be the set of vertices reachable from \(s\) in \(G_f\). Then \((S_{\min},V\setminus S_{\min})\) is a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut. Moreover, for every source side \(S\) of a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut, \(S_{\min}\subseteq S\). Consequently \(S_{\min}\) is independent of the chosen maximum flow and is the unique inclusion-minimal minimum-cut source side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual reachability from the source under any maximum flow gives the unique smallest source side among all minimum cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{\min}=R_{G_f}(s)\) is the unique inclusion-minimal source side of a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut.

notation.meaning: Residual graph of the maximum flow f.
Vertices reachable from s in the residual graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph with distinct vertices \(s,t\), let \(u:A\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\), and fix a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow \(f\) with residual graph \(G_f\). Let \(S_{\min}\) and \(S_{\max}\) be the residual extremal source sides. Every minimum-cut source side \(S\) satisfies \(S_{\min}\subseteq S\subseteq S_{\max}\). Conversely, a set \(S\subseteq V\) is a minimum-cut source side exactly when \(s\in S\), \(t\notin S\), and no residual arc of \(G_f\) leaves \(S\). Hence the minimum-cut source sides are precisely the residual-successor-closed members of \([S_{\min},S_{\max}]\); arbitrary intermediate subsets need not be minimum cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite nonnegatively capacitated source-sink network, all minimum-cut source sides lie between the two residual extremal sides, and exactly the residually closed intermediate sets are minimum cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cut Lattice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses source-side inclusion as the order on minimum source-sink cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be the family of source sides of minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cuts in a finite digraph with nonnegative capacities. If \(X,Y\in\mathcal M\), then \(X\cap Y\in\mathcal M\) and \(X\cup Y\in\mathcal M\). Therefore \((\mathcal M,\subseteq)\) is a distributive lattice whose meet and join are respectively intersection and union. Its least and greatest elements are the minimal and maximal source-side minimum cuts \(S_{\min}\) and \(S_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum-cut source sides form a distributive lattice: intersection is meet, union is join, and the residual extremal cuts are its bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal M,\cap,\cup)\) is a distributive lattice with bottom \(S_{\min}\) and top \(S_{\max}\).

notation.meaning: Family of source sides of minimum s-t cuts.
Least and greatest members of the minimum-cut family.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Strong-Component Condensation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forms the acyclic component order underlying the Picard–Queyranne representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximum flow \(f\), partition its residual graph \(G_f\) into strongly connected components and contract each component to obtain the condensation digraph \(D_f\). The graph \(D_f\) is acyclic. A vertex set \(S\subseteq V\) has no residual arc leaving it if and only if \(S\) is a union of residual strong components whose corresponding component set \(I\subseteq V(D_f)\) is successor-closed: whenever \(C\in I\) and \(CD\in A(D_f)\), one has \(D\in I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contracting residual strong components produces a DAG, and residual-closed vertex sets correspond exactly to successor-closed unions of its components.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a maximum flow in a finite capacitated digraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta^+_{G_f}(S)=\varnothing\) iff \(S=\bigcup_{C\in I}C\) for a successor-closed \(I\subseteq V(D_f)\).

notation.meaning: Strong-component condensation of the residual graph.
A set of residual strong components.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity and Reverse-Edge Bound for Minimum Mean Residual Circuits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here \(\mu(f)\) denotes the minimum mean circuit weight in the residual digraph of flow \(f\), and \(n=|V(G)|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_t\) be \(b\)-flows such that, for every \(i<t\), \(\mu(f_i)<0\) and \(f_{i+1}\) is obtained from \(f_i\) by augmenting along a minimum-mean circuit \(C_i\) of \(G_{f_i}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum Mean Cycle-Cancelling Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assumes a feasible capacitated b-flow exists; residual capacities and reverse-edge costs are those induced by the current flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start with any feasible \(b\)-flow \(f\). Repeatedly choose a circuit \(C\) of minimum mean weight in the residual digraph \(G_f\). If \(G_f\) is acyclic or \(c(C)\ge 0\), return \(f\). Otherwise set \(\gamma=\min_{e\in E(C)}u_f(e)\), augment \(f\) by \(\gamma\) along \(C\), and repeat. The returned flow is a minimum-cost \(b\)-flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with a feasible b-flow. Repeatedly augment by the minimum residual capacity along a minimum-mean residual circuit of negative cost. Stop when the residual graph is acyclic or its minimum-mean circuit has nonnegative cost; the resulting flow is a minimum-cost b-flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Maximum Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard integrality theorem for finite directed maximum-flow instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph with distinct vertices \(s,t\) and integer capacities \(u_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every \(a\in A\). Then the maximum-flow problem admits an optimal flow \(f\) satisfying \(f_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every arc. In particular, Ford–Fulkerson initialized at the zero flow and augmented along residual \(s\)-\(t\) paths preserves integrality and terminates at an integral maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite network with nonnegative integer capacities has an integer-valued maximum flow; integral augmentations preserve this property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a maximum flow \(f\) with \(f_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every \(a\in A\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Capacity Path Packings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed edge-disjoint path form of max-flow min-cut for unit capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph with distinct vertices \(s,t\), and assign capacity \(u_a=1\) to every arc. The maximum number of pairwise arc-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths equals the minimum cardinality of an arc set whose deletion destroys every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path. Equivalently, an integral maximum flow decomposes into that many arc-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) path flows plus directed cycle flows; deleting the cycles leaves an optimal path packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a unit-capacity digraph, the largest arc-disjoint source-sink path packing equals the smallest source-sink arc cut.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite digraph with \(s\ne t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{\text{arc-disjoint }s\text{-}t\text{ paths}\}=\min\{|F|:G-F\text{ has no }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\}\).

notation.meaning: An arc set separating s from t.

children.title: Fractional-Capacity Regime
children.top_down_role: Maximum-flow structure for nonintegral rational capacity data.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional-Capacity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rational scaling preserves an exact discrete integrality structure but not unscaled integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every capacity of a finite \(s\)-\(t\) network is a nonnegative rational number. Choose an integer \(D>0\) such that \(D u_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for all arcs. The scaled network has an integral maximum flow \(g\); therefore \(f=g/D\) is a maximum flow of the original network and satisfies \(f_a\in D^{-1}\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). Thus a rational maximum flow exists, although an integer-valued maximum flow need not exist in the original units.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational capacities can be scaled to integers, yielding a rational maximum flow whose denominator divides a common capacity denominator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a common denominator \(D\), some maximum flow satisfies \(f_a\in D^{-1}\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every arc.

notation.meaning: A common positive denominator of all capacities.
Integral maximum flow in the scaled network.

children.title: Arbitrary Real-Capacity Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary Real-Capacity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates max-flow existence and duality from integrality and augmenting-path termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite and let \(u:A\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) be arbitrary. The feasible-flow set is a nonempty compact polytope, so the flow-value functional attains a maximum. Max-flow min-cut duality remains valid: the maximum flow value equals the minimum capacity of an \(s\)-\(t\) cut. However, neither integer nor rational coordinates are guaranteed, and unrestricted Ford–Fulkerson augmenting-path choices are not guaranteed to terminate when capacities include irrational numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With arbitrary nonnegative real capacities, maximum flows and min-cut duality still exist, but arithmetic integrality and Ford–Fulkerson termination may fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_f |f|=\min_{s\in S,\,t\notin S}u(\delta^+(S))\), with no general integrality or unrestricted termination guarantee.

notation.meaning: Total capacity leaving the cut source side S.

children.title: Integrality Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies integer capacities as sufficient and nonintegral capacities as an immediate obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The integral maximum-flow conclusion does not extend to general nonintegral capacities. Consider the network with vertices \(s,t\) and one arc \(a=st\) of capacity \(u_a=1/2\). Its unique maximum flow has \(f_a=1/2\), so no integer-valued maximum flow exists. More generally, integral capacities guarantee an integral optimum, whereas rational capacities guarantee only an optimum on the lattice determined by a common denominator; arbitrary real capacities provide no rationality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single source-sink arc of capacity one-half already shows that nonintegral capacities need not admit an integral maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: The flow is measured in the original, unscaled capacity units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(u_{st}=1/2\), every maximum flow satisfies \(f_{st}=1/2\notin\mathbb Z\).

notation.meaning: The sole directed arc from source to sink.

children.title: Termination Boundary
children.top_down_role: Algorithmic termination issues arising beyond discrete capacity regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Termination Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the arithmetic boundary for unrestricted Ford–Fulkerson augmenting-path termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite network with rational capacities, choose a common denominator \(D\). Ford–Fulkerson started at zero and using any residual augmenting path increases the flow value by a positive multiple of \(1/D\); because the value is bounded above, only finitely many augmentations occur. This argument fails for irrational capacities: there exist finite networks with irrational capacities and sequences of augmenting-path choices producing infinitely many augmentations, possibly converging to a value strictly below the maximum. Thus unrestricted Ford–Fulkerson has a rational-capacity termination guarantee but no arbitrary-real-capacity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ford–Fulkerson always terminates for rational capacities, but suitable irrational instances and path choices can cause infinite, even suboptimal, augmentation sequences.
assumptions_latex: Ford–Fulkerson begins with the zero flow and permits arbitrary augmenting-path choices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in\mathbb Q_{ge0}^{A}\) guarantees finite termination; \(u\in\mathbb R_{ge0}^{A}\) does not.

notation.meaning: A common denominator of all rational capacities.

children.title: Circulation-Transshipment Feasibility Theory
children.top_down_role: Feasibility models, reductions, cut obstructions, and algorithms for bounded circulations and supply-demand networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Bounded Circulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite directed networks with nonnegative arc capacities and zero vertex balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph and let \(u:A\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). An upper-bounded circulation is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfying \[0\le f_a\le u_a\quad(a\in A),\qquad \sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a=0\quad(v\in V).\] Thus every vertex has equal total inflow and outflow, while each arc carries a nonnegative amount no greater than its capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper-bounded circulation respects every nonnegative arc capacity and conserves flow at every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is feasible exactly when \(0\le f\le u\) and its balance is zero at every vertex.

notation.meaning: arcs leaving and entering vertex v

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arcwise minimum-flow conditions in a two-sided bounded circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) with lower-bound vector \(\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), a flow vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfies the lower-bound requirements precisely when \[f_a\ge \ell_a\qquad\text{for every }a\in A.\] In a two-sided bounded circulation these inequalities are imposed simultaneously with flow conservation and the upper inequalities \(f_a\le u_a\). A necessary condition for an arcwise feasible interval is \(\ell_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every arc must carry at least its prescribed lower amount; each lower bound must not exceed the corresponding upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lower-bound predicate is \(f_a\ge\ell_a\) for all \(a\in A\).

notation.meaning: required minimum flow on arc a
permitted maximum flow on arc a

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Bound Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arcwise capacity conditions in a two-sided bounded circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) with upper-bound vector \(u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), a flow vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfies the upper-bound restrictions precisely when \[f_a\le u_a\qquad\text{for every }a\in A.\] In a two-sided bounded circulation these restrictions are imposed together with flow conservation and the lower inequalities \(f_a\ge\ell_a\). Hence the permissible value of an individual arc is confined to the interval \([\ell_a,u_a]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every arc flow is at most its capacity and, together with its lower bound, lies in the prescribed interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The upper-bound predicate is \(f_a\le u_a\) for all \(a\in A\).

children.title: Feasible-Interval Interaction
children.top_down_role: Combined structural effect of lower and upper arc bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Interval Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-slack representation of simultaneous lower and upper arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfy \(\ell_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\), and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\). Write \(f=\ell+x\). Then the simultaneous arc conditions \(\ell_a\le f_a\le u_a\) are equivalent to \[0\le x_a\le u_a-\ell_a\qquad(a\in A).\] If \(\partial z(v)=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}z_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}z_a\), then the balance equation \(\partial f=b\) is equivalent to \[\partial x=b-\partial\ell.\] Thus lower bounds consume capacity and shift vertex balances; nonempty arc intervals alone do not guarantee a globally feasible circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting lower bounds leaves residual capacities and shifts vertex balances; conservation still couples otherwise nonempty arc intervals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell\le f\le u\) and \(\partial f=b\) if and only if \(f=\ell+x\), \(0\le x\le u-\ell\), and \(\partial x=b-\partial\ell\).

notation.meaning: flow remaining after mandatory lower-bound flow
vertexwise outflow minus inflow of arc vector z

knowledge_statements.title: Supply-Demand Transshipments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated transshipment with positive balances interpreted as supplies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfy \(\ell\le u\), and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfy \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\). A feasible supply-demand transshipment is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) such that \[\ell_a\le f_a\le u_a\quad(a\in A),\qquad \sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a=b_v\quad(v\in V).\] Under this convention, \(b_v>0\) denotes supply and \(b_v<0\) denotes demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transshipment routes flow within arc bounds so each vertex realizes its prescribed supply or demand balance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility means \(\ell\le f\le u\) and \(\partial f=b\).

notation.meaning: net supply at vertex v under the outflow-minus-inflow convention

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Excess Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-bounded flows whose vertex excesses lie in prescribed intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite, with arc bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) and vertex excess bounds \(p,q\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\). A bounded-excess flow is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfying \[\ell_a\le f_a\le u_a\quad(a\in A),\qquad p_v\le \sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a\le q_v\quad(v\in V).\] Necessarily \(\ell\le u\), \(p\le q\), and the realized excesses sum to zero because every arc contributes once positively and once negatively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-excess flow obeys arc intervals while allowing each vertex balance to vary within its own prescribed interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is \(\{f:\ell\le f\le u,\ p\le\partial f\le q\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine reduction from two-sided bounds to zero lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given arc bounds \(\ell\le f\le u\) and vertex balances \(\partial f=b\), set \(x_a=f_a-\ell_a\) and \(c_a=u_a-\ell_a\). Then \[0\le x_a\le c_a\quad(a\in A),\qquad \partial x(v)=b_v-\partial\ell(v)\quad(v\in V).\] Conversely, every \(x\) satisfying these residual constraints yields a feasible original flow by \(f=x+\ell\). Hence the transformation is a bijection between the original feasible flows and the residual zero-lower-bound flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract every lower bound, reduce each capacity accordingly, and shift each vertex balance by the lower-bound vector's imbalance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\mapsto x=f-\ell\) bijects \(\{f:\ell\le f\le u,\partial f=b\}\) with \(\{x:0\le x\le u-\ell,\partial x=b-\partial\ell\}\).

notation.meaning: residual flow after subtracting lower bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary Source Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Super-source arcs for reducing balanced transshipment feasibility to maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{A}\), and let \(d\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfy \(\sum_{v\in V}d_v=0\), using the convention \(\partial x=d\). Create a new vertex \(s^*\). For every \(v\in V\) with \(d_v>0\), add an auxiliary arc \((s^*,v)\) with capacity \(d_v\); add no source arc when \(d_v\le0\). Retain every original arc and its capacity. Saturation of \((s^*,v)\) supplies the inflow needed for the original arcs to have net outflow \(d_v\) at \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a super-source arc of capacity equal to each positive supply, directing it into the corresponding supply vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The auxiliary-source arc set is \(A_{s^*}=\{(s^*,v):v\in V,\ d_v>0\}\), with capacity \(c_{s^*v}=d_v\) on each such arc.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Arc Saturation Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-flow certificate for feasibility of a balanced zero-lower-bound transshipment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with nonnegative capacities \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{A}\), and let \(d\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfy \(\sum_{v\in V}d_v=0\), using the balance convention \(\partial x=d\). Form the augmented network with arcs \((s^*,v)\) of capacity \(d_v\) for \(d_v>0\) and arcs \((v,t^*)\) of capacity \(-d_v\) for \(d_v<0\). Put \(D=\sum_{v\in V:d_v>0}d_v\). The original transshipment is feasible if and only if the augmented network admits an \(s^*\)-to-\(t^*\) flow of value \(D\). Equivalently, every arc leaving \(s^*\), and hence every arc entering \(t^*\), is saturated. Restricting such a flow to the original arcs certifies feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transshipment is feasible exactly when a maximum flow has total value equal to the total positive balance, thereby saturating every auxiliary source and sink arc.
assumptions_latex: The auxiliary arcs use the outflow-minus-inflow convention \(\partial x=d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is equivalent to \(\operatorname{val}(x)=D\), equivalently to saturation of all auxiliary terminal arcs.

notation.meaning: total positive balance, equal to total demand magnitude

children.title: Flow-to-Circulation Reduction
children.top_down_role: Conversion of a source-sink flow instance into a circulation instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-to-Circulation Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Return-arc encoding of a capacitated source-sink flow as a circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be an \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow of value \(
u\) in \(G=(V,A)\), so conservation holds on \(V\setminus\{s,t\}\), the net outflow at \(s\) is \(
u\), and the net inflow at \(t\) is \(
u\). Add a return arc \(e_0=(t,s)\) whose permitted interval contains \(
u\), and define \(f_a=x_a\) for \(a\in A\) and \(f_{e_0}=
u\). Then \(f\) is a circulation in the augmented graph. Thus fixing \(f_{e_0}=
u\) encodes the flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a return arc from sink to source carrying the flow value; the resulting augmented flow is a circulation.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible capacitated \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow of value \(\nu\).

knowledge_statements.title: Circulation-to-Flow Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of a source-sink flow by deleting its value-encoding return arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\), and let \(G'=(V,A\cup\{e_0\})\) be the augmented graph with distinguished return arc \(e_0=(t,s)\). Let \(f\) be a feasible circulation on \(G'\), and put \(
u=f_{e_0}\). Delete \(e_0\) and define \(x_a=f_a\) for every \(a\in A\). Conservation of \(f\) implies that \(x\) has net outflow \(
u\) at \(s\), net inflow \(
u\) at \(t\), and zero balance at every vertex in \(V\setminus\{s,t\}\). If the bounds on arcs in \(A\) are the original bounds, then \(x\) is a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow of value \(
u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete the sink-to-source return arc; its circulation amount becomes the recovered source-sink flow value.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and \(s,t\in V\) are distinct.
All arcs in \(A\) retain the original flow bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The restriction \(x=f|_A\) is an \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow with value \(\operatorname{val}(x)=f_{e_0}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Encoding Return Arc
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard reduction of a capacitated source-sink flow to a circulation by a return arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have source \(s\), sink \(t\), capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and let \(F\ge0\). Add an arc \(a_0=(t,s)\) with lower and upper bounds \(\ell(a_0)=u(a_0)=F\), leaving each original arc bounded by \(0\le x_e\le u_e\). Then restriction to \(E\) is a feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow of value \(F\) if and only if the augmented vector is a feasible circulation. More generally, if \(0\le x_{a_0}\le U\), the return-arc value equals the value of the recovered flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed return flow from the sink to the source converts a flow of prescribed value into a circulation; the return-arc flow records that value.
assumptions_latex: All capacities are finite and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x|_E\text{ has value }F\iff (x,x_{a_0}=F)\text{ is a feasible circulation}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Transshipment-to-Circulation Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encodes prescribed vertex divergences as fixed flows incident to one auxiliary vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have bounds \(\ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\) and prescribed divergences \(b:V\to\mathbb R\), where \(\sum_{v\in V}b(v)=0\) and divergence means outgoing flow minus incoming flow. Add a vertex \(r\). For each \(v\) with \(b(v)>0\), add \((r,v)\) fixed at \(b(v)\); for each \(v\) with \(b(v)<0\), add \((v,r)\) fixed at \(-b(v)\). Then \(x\) is a bounded transshipment with divergence \(b\) exactly when its extension by these fixed arcs is a bounded circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An auxiliary vertex and fixed incident arcs absorb every prescribed vertex imbalance, yielding an equivalent circulation instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{div}_x(v)=b(v)\ \forall v\in V\iff \widehat x\text{ is a circulation on the augmented graph}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Balance-Encoding Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-consistent interface between transshipment divergences and fixed auxiliary-arc flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adopt \(\operatorname{div}_x(v)=x(\delta^+(v))-x(\delta^-(v))\). A balance vector \(b\in\mathbb R^V\) is compatible with a closed transshipment instance precisely when \(\sum_{v\in V}b(v)=0\). Its circulation encoding must contribute auxiliary divergence \(-b(v)\) at every original vertex: use a fixed incoming arc of value \(b(v)\) when \(b(v)>0\), a fixed outgoing arc of value \(-b(v)\) when \(b(v)<0\), and no balance arc when \(b(v)=0\). Reversing the divergence convention reverses these arc orientations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balances must sum to zero, and each fixed auxiliary arc must contribute the negative of its vertex’s required divergence.
assumptions_latex: Divergence is defined as outgoing minus incoming flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in V}b(v)=0\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{div}_{\mathrm{aux}}(v)=-b(v)\ \forall v\in V.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Circulation Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hoffman’s finite directed bounded-circulation criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with real arc bounds \(\ell_a\le u_a\). A circulation \(x\) satisfying \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\) exists if and only if, for every subset \(S\subseteq V\),
\[
\ell(\delta^-(S))\le u(\delta^+(S)).
\]
Here bounds are summed over the indicated cut arcs. Equivalently, no vertex set requires more lower-bounded inflow than its outgoing arcs can carry. The inequalities for \(S=\varnothing\) and \(S=V\) are vacuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded circulation exists exactly when every vertex set’s mandatory incoming flow is at most its available outgoing capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_a,u_a\in\mathbb R\) and \(\ell_a\le u_a\) for every arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x:\operatorname{div}_x=0,\ \ell\le x\le u\iff \ell(\delta^-(S))\le u(\delta^+(S))\ \forall S\subseteq V.\)
